text:
The Sustainable Skies World Summit 2026 was held in Farnborough in March providing an opportunity for specialist speakers from around the world to describe, examine and debate progress in moving closer towards achieving solutions applicable to meeting challenging sustainability goals that are critical to the future of aviation. RICHARD GARDNER MRAeS reports.

When preparations were underway for Farnborough International to host this important conference to provide an in-depth update on what is being planned by industry stakeholders, poly-makers, investors and sustainability advocates, few could have imagined that the event would be taking place simultaneously with the intensification of the worst global energy crisis in decades. With attacks on strategically important Middle East oil and gas installations and the free flow of associated surface shipping halted, the resulting instability in energy costs provided a timely backdrop to underline the requirement to provide a viable pathway towards making fuel supplies more sustainable for a commercial aviation sector that is expected to carry on expanding into the future. Beyond this, the challenge remains how best to identify and develop technology solutions for an era where today’s vast fleets of commercial aircraft will require replacing.

Jet Zero Taskforce

The Minister for Aviation, Maritime and Decarbonisation gave a pre-recorded video address. (SSWS)

The conference was opened with a video-recording of Kier Mather MP, Minister for Aviation, Maritime and Decarbonisation, who announced that the first annual report of the Jet Zero Taskforce was now completed, and this was aimed at creating a plan for decarbonizing air travel. He said the key to this would be the UK’s Sustainable Aviation Fuel Mandate which was introduced last year setting out SAF blend content for fuel supplies to rise from 2% to 10% by 2030. He said this would provide a clear long-term signal to accelerate production and adoption. He added that the government plans a Revenue Certainty Mechanism designed to unlock private investment and was committing £63m through the Advanced Fuels Fund.

Sustainable Aviation’s CEO, Duncan McCurt, announced a £2m Advanced Market Signal initiative aimed at scaling the greenhouse gas market. Industry members have committed to purchasing carbon credits, supporting the market development to require 20-30m tons of carbon removals annually by 2050. In the shared investment session, Matt Ridley, Director of Sustainability and Innovation at One World, said “We must find a way to reduce the impact on the environment. Sustainable Skies is an important and inspiring opportunity to meet people from other parts of the sector and I’ve been encouraged to see how sustainability is represented and to find about their thinking. Keynotes, panel discussions and workshops have indicated much progress to date while aligning priorities and targets to shape the future.”

Mandates

Airspace Unlimited's Dr Martin Hawley called into the RAeS stand. His article 'Freedom in the skies - the reality of free route airspace' featured in the March 2026 edition of AEROSPACE. (Kelsey Baguley/RAeS)

Eddy Liegeois, Head of Aviation Policy at the European Commission, spoke about his commitment to decarbonising the sector and suggested at that at the head of the challenge were three main considerations – market-based systems, engine developments and clean aviation, including hydrogen. Air Traffic Management also needed to be optimised to better exploit the gains. He told the delegates that there was a legal obligation in Europe that fuel suppliers must meet the SAF challenge or face penalties for non-compliance. There would need to be subsidies and there was a high cost to intervention by governments for investment but that would provide more certainty and long term visibility. It was important to maintain a pipeline of projects, such as advanced biomass for fuels. The mandates will stay he said but how best to support airlines buying SAF is a factor. The 2% mandate was set in 2023 but there has been a relatively small percentage increase since then, so are the mandates working?

Greg Archer European Policy Director at Lanzatech suggested that other means of support were needed to boost the market. This was echoed by Dr Preeti Jain, Head of Net Zero Research and Programmes at IATA, who called for technology openness in looking for incentives for airlines. Compliance costs to meet mandates were expensive. Voluntary adoption of SAF levels might help better and cost operators half as much, suggested Tim Lederer, VP Regulatory Affairs Global Aviation, DHL Express. He thought free market dynamics on price discussion preferable to market decision- making. Lively debate ensued concerning the causes of the slow take up in meeting SAF targets and introducing incentives. Advanced methods aimed at increasing new sources for producing SAF, including the conversion of waste gasses, was discussed and promoted to boost long-term supply. Greg Archer thought that protracted granting permission for new proposals was resulting in delays in bringing new products to market and reducing SAF costs. There were sovereignty issues involved in sourcing crop-based feedstocks for SAF use and energy security was another international factor. Others mentioned it was a reality to face up to in that crop-based and pre-used oils were unlikely to become available in sufficient quantities to fully meet the predicted demands for long term SAF fuel production. Different markets globally take different positions on decarbonising as they have differing resources, priorities and national policies, some free-market, some mixed economies and others under state control. Supply lines will also vary considerably as well as economic stability, so decision-making will inevitably incorporate great diversity and this will impact on aviation policies and supporting capabilities. Sanjeev Sajjela, CEO at PySAF is focused on a next generation biomass biocrude platform which converts agricultural and forestry residues into refinery-ready intermediates for SAF and marine fuels. Peter Goult, Director at Project Sky Power, spoke of clean energy investment and 40 new projects, 10 of which were advanced with results expected by 2030. 2.4 billion Euros would be invested in emerging mechanisms. The model would see the establishment of long-term supply which would be re-sold to markets. There was a strategic imperative in searching for a way forward.

Airspace modernisation

RAeS Executive Committee Member Richard Wilson MRAeS led a session updating progress on next generation aircraft. (Jonathan Clare/RAeS)

Ian Jopson Director of Sustainability at NATS pointed out that the UK dealt with over 6,500 air traffic movements daily and air space modernisation was an important factor in cutting emissions alongside the deployment of more fuel efficient aircraft. Progress was being made in data collection and measurement and this helped plan mitigation and best practise. Many ATM questions were discussed in a Q&A session relating to contrail reductions and exploiting optimum operations for different categories of aircraft and services flying at different altitudes. Future use of AI will assist in dealing with congestion, along with trials, in better matching carbon reducing flights while operations continue to grow. While safety remains paramount congestion issues will compromise the full optimisation of flights and airlines may have to trade time and fuel to reduce emissions and that will impact on operating costs.

RAeS at SSWS26

RAeS Past President, Kerissa Khan FRAeS, acted as Session Chair on Sustainable Solutions. (SSWS)

The Royal Aeronautical Society was a Corporate Partner at SSWS26 and as well having a presence in the networking area, many Society members were participants or delegates at the event.

In addition, Past President Kerissa Khan FRAeS, now Future Flight Innovation Lead at UKRI, acted as Session Chair on Sustainable Solutions. This examined the coming introduction of e-VTOL and Urban Mobility aircraft and addressed the question, “Sustainable Solution or Luxury Distraction?” Simon Meakins from Bristow discussed how the economic model might work and addressed aspects of practicality.

The session on updating progress on next generation aircraft was led by Society Executive Committee Member Richard Wilson MRAeS. This session was extremely wide ranging with expertise contributed by Ash Owen, Head of Future Technology at Rolls-Royce, Nicholas Earl, VP Safran UK, David Debrey, Head of Technology Whole Aircraft Aerospace Technology, at the Aerospace Technology Institute, and Jonathan Chestney, RISE Technical Director at Dowty (GEAerospace UK). A theme was generating maximum energy most efficiently from new engine designs. There was a consensus that today’s narrow body size category of commercial airliner would still comprise the biggest market well through the coming decades, and beyond, and a next generation of both open-fan and ultra-fan engines would power them. New materials, new manufacturing processes and new engines would significantly improve efficiency and reduce emissions. Bringing down all-up aircraft weight would deliver better performance all-round. Today’s aircraft interiors were getting heavier with on-board at-seat services and complex seats, and this would be overcome with new generation interior solutions. More electric power would also be generated by on-board systems reducing much power currently off-loaded from the engines. More composite manufacturing at scale was coming and all options were on the table, such as folding wings to allow wide airport use.

Hydrogen fuel cells and hybridisation were also discussed in some detail as were the infrastructure and supply implications of slowly moving towards these radical technologies. There was general agreement that maturing these possibilities for commercial service was still a long way into the future other than for taking small steps forward starting with small, short-range aircraft. Providing enough suitable hydrogen or electric power on the ground to sustain intensive airport operations, on a large and international scale, allowing for rapid turn-rounds and commercial viability, suggested replacing less radical fuel supplies was still a long way off. But this conference certainly provided a wealth of new information, even if there were more questions than answers.

The Society welcomes the opportunity to support these conversations and contribute to shaping a more sustainable, resilient aerospace sector for generations to come. We look forward to hosting our Sustainability Summit on 22-23 June 2026 at No.4 Hamilton Place.

text:
The London Laurel County Economic Development Authority, Ecostrat and the BDO Zone Initiative are pleased to announce the issue of a BDO Zone ‘A’ Rating for Laurel County, Kentucky. The BDO Zone is rated for 342,000 bone dry tons per year of low-risk woody biomass and spans a 75-mile drive radius from its central point in London, Kentucky.

This rating was funded by the Kentucky Energy and Environment Cabinet’s Office of Energy Policy through State Energy Program funds made available under the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act.

Laurel County’s ‘A’ rating indicates high prospective viability to support new biobased plant operations, with low risk associated with Feedstock Supply and Infrastructure in the Zone. Declining regional demand for pulpwood and certain sawmill residuals has created an opportunity for new facilities to utilize underused resources, with pulpwood prices currently at historic lows. Kentucky’s mandated professional logger certification program further supports a reliable and environmentally responsible supply chain. Together with a nearby project development site—located within six miles of downtown London and offering natural gas, three-phase power, high-speed internet, and heavy industrial zoning—the region is well positioned to support new bio-based manufacturing investment.

Paula Thompson, Executive Director of the London Laurel County Economic Development Authority, stated, “Our ‘A’ rating highlights the significant economic potential of our woody biomass resources. By partnering with biobased companies, we aim to expand our value chain, attract new investment, and create high-quality jobs while positioning our region as a leader in bio-based manufacturing.”

Kenya Stump, Executive Director of the Kentucky Office of Energy Policy, stated, “This rating highlights Kentucky’s resources and desire to be an innovative force in the biofuels space. Fuel diversification is a key pillar of Kentucky’s Energy Strategy, and by supporting our existing forestry and agricultural sectors we can unlock new opportunities for rural economic development. Laurel County’s strong feedstock availability and infrastructure position the region to attract investment in biobased manufacturing and help strengthen Kentucky’s role in the emerging bioeconomy.”

title: Europe faces flight cancellations as Strait of Hormuz closure triggers jet fuel crisis
description:
European airports are facing severe shortages of jet fuel in the coming weeks if the Strait of Hormuz is not reopened as soon as possible, an industry body has said.
ACI Europe, a trade body representing airports around Europe, has written to EU transport commissioner Apostolos Tzitzikostas expressing “increasing concern” about the shortage of the fuel.
While some larger European airports such as Heathrow have storage tankers on-site, this is generally only enough for around seven days of flights at the absolute maximum.
In the letter seen by The Financial Times, ACI Europe said that reserves across European airports are running low and suppliers are unable to guarantee deliveries beyond the coming weeks.

European airports are facing severe shortages of jet fuel in the coming weeks if the Strait of Hormuz is not reopened as soon as possible, an industry body has said.

ACI Europe, a trade body representing airports around Europe, has written to EU transport commissioner Apostolos Tzitzikostas expressing “increasing concern” about the shortage of the fuel. It warns that large numbers of flights face cancellation within weeks.

In the letter, ACI called for “proactive EU monitoring and action” to ensure the aviation sector was getting the fuel it needed, which includes identifying alternative import sources.

In recent decades, aviation has become increasingly reliant on the Middle East for its jet fuel supplies due to closures of older refineries in the West and the opening of state-of-the-art ‘mega refineries’ along the strait. In particular, the Al-Zour Refinery in Kuwait has a processing capacity of 615,000 barrels per day and is one of the largest refineries in the world. However, it is reliant on the Strait to export its product to Europe and the West and is currently blocked from doing so.

While some larger European airports such as Heathrow have storage tankers on-site, this is generally only enough for around seven days of flights at the absolute maximum.

In the letter seen by The Financial Times, ACI Europe said that reserves across European airports are running low and suppliers are unable to guarantee deliveries beyond the coming weeks.

“If the passage through the Strait of Hormuz does not resume in any significant and stable way within the next three weeks, [a] systemic jet fuel shortage is set to become a reality for the EU,” the letter stated.

“The fact that we are entering the peak summer season ... is only adding to those concerns. This crisis has exposed the reduced refining capacity of the EU for jet fuel production, and its acute dependence on imports from other world regions.”

The current shortage bolsters the case for escalating production of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), which is typically derived from waste and renewable feedstocks such as used cooking oil, animal fats and agricultural waste.

“Additional support for SAF is also about strategic autonomy, which the current crisis is even more bringing to the fore,” ACI Europe said.

text:
The USDA maintained its forecast for 2025-’26 soybean oil use in biofuel production in its latest World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates report, released April 9. The estimated season-average price for soybean oil was revised up.

The current outlook for U.S. soybean supply and use for 2025-’26 includes higher crush, lower exports and unchanged ending stocks. Soybean crush is raised 35 million bushels to 2.61 billion on increased soybean meal domestic use. Exports are reduced 4.54 million bushels to 1.54 billion on pace to date and higher South American shipments. Soybean ending stocks are unchanged at 350 million bushels.

The USDA maintained its forecast that 14 billion pounds of soybean oil will go to biofuel production in 2025-’26, up from an estimated 11.758 billion pounds in 2024-’25. Soybean oil use for biofuel production was at 12.995 billion pounds for 2023-’24.

The U.S. season-average soybean price for 2025-’26 is forecast at $10.30 per bushel, up 10 cents. The soybean meal price is increased $10 to $310 per short ton and the soybean oil price is raised 4 cents to 59 cents per pound.

Global 2025-‘26 soybean supply includes higher beginning stocks and production. Beginning stocks are raised 1 million tons mainly on a revised 2024-‘25 crop for Brazil. After a review of 2025 disappearance data, Brazil’s 2024-'25 production is raised 1 million tons to 172.5 million. Soybean production for 2025-‘26 is raised 200,000 tons on higher crops for Paraguay and South Africa partly offset by a lower crop for Uruguay.

Global 2025-‘26 soybean use includes nearly unchanged exports, higher crush, and lower ending stocks. Increased soybean exports for Brazil and Paraguay are mostly offset by lower exports for the United States and Uruguay. Soybean crush is increased for the United States, Brazil, and Algeria. Global soybean ending stocks are reduced 500,000 tons to 124.8 million, mainly on lower stocks for Argentina, Brazil, and Egypt.

title: Scheme launched to provide independent verification of SAF traceability in the UK
description:

Valero Energy is the first SAF supplier to be approved under RFAS Aviation.
Zemo has developed a standardised SAF Declaration, enabling fuel suppliers to provide verified SAF production pathway, feedstock and lifecycle GHG emissions data.
Open to companies supplying SAF to the UK aviation sectors, RFAS Aviation aims to enable consistent and credible communication of SAF attributes to customers and strengthen transparency as SAF volumes increase in the UK fuel mix, adds Zemo.

text:
The absence of a consistent mechanism to verify sustainable aviation fuel traceability has limited the ability of airline operators to demonstrate GHG emissions reductions under the UK Emissions Trading Scheme and of fuel suppliers to provide robust evidence of SAF sustainability credentials to customers. So claims the not-for-profit Zemo Partnership, which has launched RFAS Aviation, a new voluntary assurance scheme designed to provide independent verification of SAF across the UK supply chain. The initiative builds on the established Renewable Fuels Assurance Scheme (RFAS), which Zemo, formerly Low Carbon Vehicle Partnership, says is widely used in the road transport sector and has approved 58 companies across the UK and Europe. Valero Energy is the first SAF supplier to be approved under RFAS Aviation.

Zemo says the scheme introduces a mechanism for verifying the traceability of SAF from the point of blending with conventional aviation fuel and then across the UK distribution network to the airport. Zemo has developed a standardised SAF Declaration, enabling fuel suppliers to provide verified SAF production pathway, feedstock and lifecycle GHG emissions data.

“This SAF Declaration serves a trusted, auditable record that can be used by airline operators to support emissions reduction claims under the UK ETS, while also enhancing transparency and confidence across the aviation fuel supply chain,” says Zemo.

Gloria Esposito, Director of Sustainable Business, said Zemo Partnership had closely collaborated with the Environment Agency, one of the UK regulators for the UK ETS, to ensure SAF Declarations aligned with UK ETS requirements and supported credible emission reduction claims.

Open to companies supplying SAF to the UK aviation sectors, RFAS Aviation aims to enable consistent and credible communication of SAF attributes to customers and strengthen transparency as SAF volumes increase in the UK fuel mix, adds Zemo. It is also designed to prevent cross-market attribution to aviation claims by ensuring kerosene supplied for other uses, such as heating, is excluded.

Zemo’s membership includes representatives of automotive and fuel supply chains, vehicle users, academics and environment groups.

title: Growing jet traffic at Flying Cloud complicates Eden Prairie climate goals
description:

That compares to 150,738 operations last year at Flying Cloud Airport.

text:
Tim Conners is all-in on sustainability and combating climate change.

He drives a plug-in hybrid electric vehicle, outfitted his Eden Prairie home with an energy-efficient heat pump and solar panels, serves on the city’s Sustainability Commission, advocates for federal carbon pricing policy through his work with the Citizens’ Climate Lobby, and helps organize the A.M. Rotary Club’s EcoExpo, an April 18 public event that will promote environmental awareness and activism.

The rest of us? Reducing waste, buying more energy-efficient appliances, swapping incandescent light bulbs for LEDs, and following other advice in the City of Eden Prairie’s six-year-old Climate Action Plan (CAP) makes us a little bit like Tim Conners. Makes us feel like we’re all in this together. All working on that CAP goal to have net-zero carbon emissions, community-wide, by 2050.

But it doesn’t really feel like we’re all together fighting climate change when fossil-fuel emissions are headed in the opposite direction just down the road, at Flying Cloud Airport.

Flying Cloud is a bit of a blind spot, at least for the moment, when it comes to the city’s climate plan and the Metropolitan Airports Commission’s (MAC) sustainability goals.

Neither the city nor MAC have measured the aircraft carbon emissions at Flying Cloud Airport or addressed how they might be reduced, although MAC is in the early stages of accrediting its six reliever airports, including Flying Cloud, through the Airport Carbon Accreditation (ACA) program run by the Airports Council International organization. MAC has achieved Level 1 of the program, but only later, in Level 3, will it begin addressing emissions from private aircraft, including business jets, at Flying Cloud.

Meanwhile, a new, long-term operating plan for Flying Cloud, approved last September by MAC, predicts that the number of small jets based at the Eden Prairie airport will increase from 30 to 71 between 2021 and 2041.

And yet, the plan’s forecast for 2030 — when 48 jet aircraft are anticipated to be based at Flying Cloud — has already been exceeded. A list of Flying Cloud aircraft registered with the Minnesota Department of Transportation (MnDOT) puts the current number of jets at 53, including jets belonging to C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Life Time Fitness, Polaris, Cambria, and MyPillow. The airport is home to 440 aircraft overall, according to MnDOT.

It’s probably no surprise, therefore, that the amount of fuel delivered annually to Flying Cloud for jet use is trending upward, reaching nearly 3.5 million gallons last year. A Beechcraft 400 jet of the type listed as owned by Cambria can seat up to eight passengers, cost upward of $1 million, and burn roughly 200 gallons of fuel per hour.

And then there are the additional jets that come with special events, such as the dozens of additional private jets landing, parking, and taking off at Flying Cloud Airport during the 2016 Ryder Cup golf tournament at Hazeltine National Golf Club in Chaska or the 2018 Super Bowl at U.S. Bank Stadium in Minneapolis. (The Ryder Cup returns to Hazeltine in 2029.)

That means at least some of the hard-earned cuts in fossil-fuel emissions that result from residents’ work on the city’s climate plan are being offset by private jets at Flying Cloud. And, it calls into question whether the city can achieve its goal of net-zero carbon emissions community-wide by 2050 if the picture of Eden Prairie’s carbon footprint is incomplete by omitting data from Flying Cloud aircraft.

In fact, the city’s climate plan doesn’t mention the reliever airport at all, limiting its section labeled “vehicle travel” to emissions from on-road vehicle traffic.

City officials say there’s a good reason why aircraft are not a focus of their plan. It’s because there are national standards and protocols for writing local government plans that address greenhouse-gas emissions. When it comes to local airports, those guidelines put the focus on emissions from electricity and natural-gas use in airport buildings, but not on emissions from aircraft themselves.

“Typically, it does not include air travel,” explained Jennifer Fierce, the city’s sustainability coordinator, “because a) cities do not have reliable access to data to calculate jet emissions, b) accounting for airport emissions usually happens at a state or national scale due to the complexity attributing emissions to specific cities, and c) airports are outside our area of influence.”

“We lack any influence over operations on Federal Aviation Administration (FAA)-regulated airports like Flying Cloud or to any associated data with respect to emissions,” she added. “This makes it challenging to include them in a local CAP because the data isn’t readily accessible and any strategies to influence emission reductions are superseded by the authority granted to the airport through the FAA.”

Instead, the city’s plan prioritizes reducing emissions in city operations and in the residential and commercial sectors, Fierce added.

“We’re focused on the priorities in the CAP as those have the biggest impact on local emissions,” she noted. “Existing building stock is 59% and transportation is 39% of our emissions, so those are really our priority sectors for emissions reduction.”

Neither do the MAC’s sustainability goals specifically mention Flying Cloud Airport or the other relievers within the orbit of Minneapolis-St. Paul International Airport. Instead, MAC’s goals focus primarily on MSP, where MAC can have the greatest impact.

Private jets high in per-passenger emissions

In Eden Prairie, Flying Cloud Airport stands apart. It’s a significant jobs driver and contributes to Eden Prairie’s economy. Flying Cloud and other MAC-owned airports are generally exempt from property tax. Privately leased individual hangars do pay property taxes, administered in the form of a personal property account.

The local airport, consisting of about 470 acres “inside the gates,” is also largely pre-empted from city ordinances. MAC and the FAA have the power to manage, operate, and control Flying Cloud. City input is largely advisory, though the city can regulate land uses surrounding Flying Cloud.

Meanwhile, the airport’s growth is closely tied to private jets, which have become a target of criticism worldwide because of their high emissions per passenger.

Although private jets represent a small fraction of overall aviation activity worldwide, they disproportionately contribute to emissions, releasing up to 14 times more CO2 per passenger than commercial jets and 50 times more than trains, according to Andrew Murphy and Valentin Simon in a study published in 2021 in Transport & Environment and headlined, “Private jets: can the super rich supercharge zero-emission aviation?”

Last year, the International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT) estimated that a private jet emits about 810 tons of greenhouse-gas emissions in a typical year, equivalent to 177 passenger cars.

But general-aviation airports like Flying Cloud, which come in different sizes and ownership structures across the U.S., are only beginning to address these private-jet emissions. A few efforts stand out.

In its Climate Action Plan, the City of Hillsboro, Oregon, population 106,477 and about 30 minutes west of Portland, takes into account the emissions from fuel use at Hillsboro Airport: An estimated 7% of all transportation emissions in the community come from the general-aviation reliever airport, which accommodates a mix of aircraft, including business jets, and has a 6,600-foot-long runway compared to Flying Cloud’s longest runway, 5,000 feet.

While Hillsboro’s climate plan outlines no strategies specific to lowering airport emissions, the Port of Portland, which owns the airport, has a goal of net zero carbon emissions by 2050 by transitioning to lead-free fuel and pushing for development of a sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) made from a variety of renewable feedstocks.

Santa Monica, California, with a 2020 population of 93,076, has the same goal as Eden Prairie: carbon neutrality by 2050. In 2015, it estimated that aviation fuel was responsible for 2% of Santa Monica’s overall carbon emissions. But it has a unique agreement with the FAA to close its reliever airport at the end of 2028, after which it will become a large public park and recreational area.

The City of Scottsdale, Arizona, is updating the 20-year master plan for its municipal airport, which acts as a reliever to the Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport. A facility for corporate jets, Scottsdale Airport had nearly 165,000 takeoffs and landings last year. That compares to 150,738 operations last year at Flying Cloud Airport.

One of Scottsdale’s objectives is to incorporate sustainability analyses and measures throughout the plan, and formulate a sustainability program that will guide future airport decision-making. Another goal is to make a technological pivot by catering its adjacent commercial-industrial business park to companies that are developing electric-powered aircraft.

Environmental concerns can also stymie airport expansion. The prospect of more private-jet flights and higher carbon emissions has sparked citizen opposition to a plan for 17-27 new hangars and additional fuel-storage capacity at Hanscom Field, which is New England’s largest general-aviation airport and located in Bedford, Massachusetts. The project is currently in limbo after the Massachusetts Environmental Policy Act (MEPA) Office ruled that the project’s Draft Environmental Impact Report (DEIR) failed to comply with regulations.

Solutions: electric jets and alternative fuels

If MAC and Eden Prairie officials were to tackle emissions at Flying Cloud Airport, what might that look like?

Among MAC’s forecasted improvements at Flying Cloud are better taxiways to reduce the time between jet parking and takeoff and vice versa. That’s one way to reduce emissions, says John Welbes, strategic communications coordinator for MAC.

Other possibilities are technology-related. For example, a 2024 limited study in Europe identified electric-powered jets as a promising solution to the high emissions per passenger from today’s fossil-fuel-powered models. It concluded that with fully electric aircraft the studied business carrier could significantly reduce its annual emissions by up to 93%, though flights would take longer.

While commercial availability of electric private jets in the U.S. is considered to be several years away, at best, more headway is coming from alternative fuels as a way to reduce aircraft emissions.

SAF is a safe and certified alternative jet fuel that can cut carbon emissions of jet fuel by more than 80%, compared to conventional jet fuel. It can be produced from a number of sources, including feedstock such as waste oil and fats, municipal waste, and non-food crops. It is “sustainable” because the raw feedstock does not compete with food crops or water supplies, and is not responsible for forest degradation.

Currently, SAF must be blended with conventional jet fuel, with blending limits ranging from 5% to 50% to meet the technical standards to ensure SAF is safe, high-quality, and compatible with aircraft.

Minnesota has a number of SAF initiatives. For example, businesses, universities, cities, counties, and others have joined to create the Minnesota SAF Hub, the nation’s first large-scale hub committed to scaling production of sustainable aviation fuel to replace conventional jet fuel.

In 2024, for the first time, a 7,000-gallon shipment of SAF made from winter camelina grown in Minnesota and North Dakota, processed by Cargill and refined by Montana Renewables, LLC, arrived at MSP Airport, where it entered the MSP fuel supply.

That same year, Delta Airlines and the Minnesota SAF Hub announced plans for the first blending facility in Minnesota in collaboration with Delta and Flint Hills Resources. The facility will blend up to 30 million gallons of SAF at its Pine Bend Refinery in Minnesota and is being constructed, with operations expected to begin in 2026.

However, the cost of producing SAF remains significantly higher than fossil-based jet fuel, primarily due to high feedstock costs, the early-stage nature of the technologies, and limited economies of scale.

Conners, the retiree, Sustainability Commission member, and climate activist, concedes that Flying Cloud Airport may be a blind spot in Eden Prairie’s climate efforts. But he adds that the city’s limited power to regulate the airport makes it more logical for MAC to be the one to enact change, since its actions could impact all six reliever airports, not just Flying Cloud.

Overall, he feels the city is doing some nice things on the sustainability front.

“Do I kind of wish we were more aggressive? Yeah,” says Conners. “Am I encouraged? Yeah. We’re a leader in the metro area, along with a few other suburbs and Minneapolis, in terms of how progressive we are on the topic, and causing change.

“I feel pretty good about that.”

text:
The Government has announced measures to accelerate planning and regulatory approvals for two major clean energy projects - Sizewell C and Lighthouse Green Fuels - by appointing the Environment Agency as Lead Environmental Regulator.

Under this approach, the Environment Agency will act as a single point of contact to coordinate environmental advice across regulators. The aim is to streamline processes, reduce delays and costs, and maintain environmental standards through more joined-up working.

Sizewell C, a new nuclear power station, is expected to supply electricity to around six million homes. During peak construction, the project is anticipated to support approximately 17,000 direct and indirect jobs, including 1,500 apprenticeships.

April 13, 2026

Advocacy by NBAA, with support from the Wisconsin Business Aviation Association (WiBAA), recently culminated with Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers signing an innovative bill to further the development and production of sustainable aviation fuels (SAF) in the Badger State.

Assembly Bill 619 authorizes the Wisconsin Economic Development Corporation to create a manufacturing zone to support production of aviation biofuel derived from woody biomass, including trees and tree limbs, needles, leaves and forestry residues.

“An SAF producer’s tax credit will support job growth and energy security,” the two associations wrote last year in support of the measure. “General aviation alone contributes 26,700 jobs and $6.5 billion in total economic output to Wisconsin. The SAF credit will support additional jobs in agriculture, forestry, infrastructure, construction, transportation and research and development.” The bill further allocates up to $120 million in tax credits for a company to produce SAF derived at least 80% from Wisconsin-sourced woody feedstocks over five years.

Lawmakers agreed, noting in the bill that, “The manufacturing of aviation biofuels in this state is essential to maintain and grow the forest products industry in this state and to create jobs.” They further called support for growing the aviation biofuels industry, “a statewide responsibility of statewide dimension.”

“On behalf of NBAA and our partners at WiBAA, we thank Gov. Evers and state legislators for taking this positive step toward greater sustainability of our nation’s aviation industry,” said NBAA Regional Director Kristi Ivey. “This bill helps make the U.S. a global leader in SAF production while also bringing new jobs to Wisconsin’s rural communities.”

“We’re very pleased to see AB619 signed into law and the strong signal it sends for advancing sustainable aviation fuel in Wisconsin,” said NBAA Environmental Committee Co-Chair Nancy Bsales. “It’s incredible to see Wisconsin support SAF growth in the state and our country, and this is a great example of state level initiatives that will help scale SAF.”

The new law reflects a key theme underscored by the industry’s CLIMBING. FAST. advocacy campaign: business aviation is an incubator for sustainability innovation, with a united goal to achieve net-zero emissions from aviation by 2050. Equally important, the industry plays an essential role in creating jobs, driving economic activity, connecting communities and providing humanitarian lift for citizens and towns in times of crisis.

text:
Six weeks of war in the Middle East have devastated lives, destroyed infrastructure and sent shockwaves through global oil markets. The aviation industry has been especially hard hit. There’s an unexpected structural consequence of this – the price gap between conventional jet fuel and sustainable alternatives is closing faster than anyone expected.

The conflict has extended far beyond the immediate region. In nine days, 37,000 flights were cancelled. This cost Gulf carriers $1 billion, while rerouting added 206,000 km of daily detours and wiped out an estimated $600 million a day in tourism revenue. Refinery strikes and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz pushed jet fuel prices to more than double.

Airlines have started to shift the burden to consumers. United Airlines warns that higher prices would add $11 billion to its fuel bill in 2026, which could push fares up by 20%.

Fuel surcharges are rising, with some London-Sydney return flights now carrying a $800 fuel surcharge. Average global airfares are at their highest since 2019 at $465. United, Air New Zealand and SAS have all announced capacity cuts.

These price dynamics are reshaping another market.

We wrote in our Solar Supercycle analysis that inflection points for new technologies occur when new tech becomes cheaper than the incumbent. The sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) premium over conventional jet fuel in Europe fell from $1,463 per metric ton before the conflict to $1,139 by mid-March.

The picture is more nuanced: most SAF today is derived from biological feedstocks – cooking oils, animal fats, biomass and alcohols – rather than synthetic e-fuels made with renewable electricity. All of these are sensitive to energy prices, whether through feedstock costs or electricity costs. Even though the gap is closing, SAF prices in Europe rose from $2,300 per metric ton in February to $2,500 in March.

SAF represented just 0.6% of jet fuel in 2025 and is expected to rise to 0.8% this year. A move towards e-SAFs could decouple jet fuel from oil – and force an early inflection point.

Thanks for reading.

According to CNBC reporting and industry pricing data, U.S. jet fuel prices have nearly doubled in recent weeks, rising from approximately $2.50 per gallon in late February to nearly $4.90 per gallon by early April, reflecting one of the most rapid fuel price increases in recent years. At the same time, limited tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has significantly constrained physical flow of crude oil and refined products. These events are once again exposing the structural vulnerability of aviation fuel supply chains that depend on geopolitically exposed crude oil markets.

In contrast, waste‑based SAF produced in the United States relies on domestically sourced feedstocks such as used cooking oil and other waste materials that are not tied to crude oil extraction, refining, or international shipping routes. At the feedstock level, these inputs are largely insulated from the supply shocks and geopolitical risks currently affecting global petroleum markets.

"When jet fuel prices can nearly double in a matter of weeks, it exposes just how fragile crude‑based aviation fuel supply chains remain," said Chris Cooper, Chief Executive Officer of XCF Global. "Waste‑based SAF starts with domestic materials, domestic infrastructure, and domestic labor. That structural difference matters, not only for decarbonization, but for fuel security and reliability when global energy systems are under stress.

XCF Global's perspective builds on the company's March statement addressing the initial impacts of Middle East‑related disruptions on aviation fuel markets. Since then, volatility has continued, with airlines confronting continued uncertainty around fuel pricing and availability.

While SAF prices can reflect broader market dynamics, the underlying supply chain for waste‑based SAF remains structurally distinct from petroleum jet fuel. Crude oil disruptions affect conventional jet fuel immediately and directly, while waste‑based SAF is not exposed to the same upstream risks, providing a meaningful layer of supply‑chain resilience.

We believe domestic SAF production represents a near‑term opportunity to reduce both carbon intensity and geopolitical exposure for the aviation industry."

text:
The Minnesota Bio-Fuels Association (MN Bio-Fuels) is encouraging fuel retailers to apply for new grant funding from the Minnesota Department of Agriculture’s (MDA) Agricultural Growth, Research, and Innovation (AGRI) Bio-Fuels Infrastructure Program to expand access to E15, also known as Unleaded 88.

MDA announced $4.7 million in grant funding is available to support fuel retailers in upgrading infrastructure to offer higher blends of ethanol. The program is funded through a legislative appropriation along with additional support from Minnesota Corn.

Eligible retailers may apply for grants ranging from $5,000 to $199,000 per project to support equipment, installation, and related infrastructure upgrades. Applicants must operate in Minnesota, have no more than 20 retail locations, and provide a minimum 35% cash match.

Brian Werner, executive director of MN Bio-Fuels, said the funding comes at an important time as retailers look to meet growing demand for lower-cost fuel options.

“This funding provides a meaningful opportunity for fuel retailers across Minnesota to expand access to Unleaded 88 and meet growing consumer demand for lower-cost fuel options,” Werner said. “At a time when gas prices remain volatile, investments in infrastructure like this help ensure more Minnesotans can access a fuel that is consistently priced lower while supporting our state’s farmers and rural economy. Expanding availability starts with making it easier for retailers to offer it.”

The program prioritizes retailers that do not currently offer higher ethanol blends and projects that expand availability across all dispensers, helping increase access statewide. There are currently 551 stations in Minnesota that offer Unleaded 88.

A recent study found Minnesota drivers saved $24.7 million in 2024 alone by choosing Unleaded 88, with $79.5 million in cumulative savings since 2013.

According to CNBC reporting and industry pricing data, U.S. jet fuel prices have nearly doubled in recent weeks, rising from approximately $2.50 per gallon in late February to nearly $4.90 per gallon by early April, reflecting one of the most rapid fuel price increases in recent years. At the same time, limited tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has significantly constrained physical flow of crude oil and refined products. These events are once again exposing the structural vulnerability of aviation fuel supply chains that depend on geopolitically exposed crude oil markets.

In contrast, waste‑based SAF produced in the United States relies on domestically sourced feedstocks such as used cooking oil and other waste materials that are not tied to crude oil extraction, refining, or international shipping routes. At the feedstock level, these inputs are largely insulated from the supply shocks and geopolitical risks currently affecting global petroleum markets.

"When jet fuel prices can nearly double in a matter of weeks, it exposes just how fragile crude‑based aviation fuel supply chains remain," said Chris Cooper, Chief Executive Officer of XCF Global. "Waste‑based SAF starts with domestic materials, domestic infrastructure, and domestic labor. That structural difference matters, not only for decarbonization, but for fuel security and reliability when global energy systems are under stress.

XCF Global's perspective builds on the company's March statement addressing the initial impacts of Middle East‑related disruptions on aviation fuel markets. Since then, volatility has continued, with airlines confronting continued uncertainty around fuel pricing and availability.

While SAF prices can reflect broader market dynamics, the underlying supply chain for waste‑based SAF remains structurally distinct from petroleum jet fuel. Crude oil disruptions affect conventional jet fuel immediately and directly, while waste‑based SAF is not exposed to the same upstream risks, providing a meaningful layer of supply‑chain resilience.

XCF Global is an emerging U.S. sustainable aviation fuel producer, with a permitted nameplate capacity of 38 million gallons per year of neat SAF at its New Rise Renewables facility in Reno, Nevada, potentially capable of supporting up to 100 million gallons of blended SAF depending on blend ratios. The facility is currently undergoing a planned turnaround as part of ongoing equipment upgrades designed to enhance long‑term reliability and performance.

"This moment is not just a reminder of why SAF matters for emissions reduction," Cooper added. "It is also a reminder that energy security starts at the origin of the fuel. We believe domestic SAF production represents a near‑term opportunity to reduce both carbon intensity and geopolitical exposure for the aviation industry."

As global energy markets navigate continued instability, XCF Global remains focused on strengthening domestic SAF infrastructure and advancing a fuel supply model that supports resilient aviation operations while contributing to long‑term decarbonization goals.

text:
Sustainable Aviation Fuel Could Buffer Airlines from Energy Spikes

by Robert Silk (Travel Weekly) Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) isn't a topic that generates exciting headlines. But one of the many lessons from the oil shock of the Iran war is that SAF matters, and not only because it's critical to decarbonize aviation. It also matters because travelers and airlines, in the U.S. and around the world, will be less exposed to energy price jolts if SAF production reaches scale.

In the U.S., approximately 300 million gallons of SAF was produced in 2025, up about two-and-a-half times from 2024, according to Ethanol Producer magazine. In relative terms, that number is small. U.S. airlines consume approximately 20 billion gallons of fuel per year.

But industry insiders fear that SAF production levels could actually decrease this year without a renewed incentive push from the federal government.

Fortunately, it's a problem that a pair of bipartisan bills, one introduced in the House in December and the other introduced in the Senate in February, would tackle.

Under a program that ended in 2024, SAF purchasers were able to claim credits of up to $1.75 per gallon for SAF. In its place is a program delineated in last summer's "One Big Beautiful Bill," which provides a credit to producers but caps it at $1 per gallon, the same amount as is provided for production of other clean fuels, most notably renewable diesel.

In refineries, SAF competes with renewable diesel, but absent additional incentives it doesn't stand much of a chance. The market for SAF is smaller. And renewable diesel production already benefits from economies of scale that SAF does not. With SAF right now costing more than $7.50 per gallon on the U.S. West Coast, according to the Argus Fuel Index, it needs the demand boost that would come from lower prices.

Absent the extra tax credit, producers are likely to dedicate their limited refinery space more heavily toward renewable diesel.

A few producers in the U.S. emphasize SAF, most notably Montana Renewables, which expects an expansion of its Great Falls facility to increase its production pace from 30 million gallons per year currently to up to 150 million gallons per by the end of this year.

But the biggest sources of last year's SAF production surge were launches by Phillips 66 and Valero.

Members of Congress recognize the potential for SAF production to flag, even as airlines have sounded the whistle about the peril of not being able to achieve the global target of net-zero airline emissions by 2050 as well as shorter-term emissions-reductions goals.

The House and Senate bills would restore the SAF credit to a maximum of $1.75 per gallon and extend it through 2033. The expected result would be demand for SAF increasing on the back of lower prices.

"It will provide confidence for new investors and production facilities," Scott Lewis, a division president for World Energy, which in February entered into a SAF transport logistics agreement with Montana Renewables, told me.

Lewis also offered what I consider some good news. Despite the U.S. political climate that has shifted away from green initiatives, World Energy hasn't seen dampened demand from corporate customers, which make SAF purchase commitments as part of their own carbon reduction goals.

description:

By 2035, Africa should be able to refine 3 000 000 bbl/d, in the process creating 500 000 direct and 2 000 000 indirect jobs and retain $100-billion in value in Africa.
text:
African industrialisation needs secure energy supply chains. So highlighted African Refiners and Distributors Association (ARDA) executive secretary Anibor Kragha in a concise address to the 2026 ARDA Conference, being held at the Century City Conference Centre in Cape Town.

ARDA, which had 80 members, championed African energy security, he affirmed. The new normal for the world today was a series of international political crises, which had nothing to do with Africa, and which were causing countries to prioritise their own interests.

Africa exported a lot of oil but still imported a lot of its fuel. "To ensure security, you need fuel," he observed.

A robust downstream sector was going to be essential for African industrialisation. "Mines run on diesel, not crude [oil]," he noted.

East and Southern Africa were heavily reliant on fuel product supply from the Middle East. West Africa was suffering less disruption because of Nigeria's giant Dangote refinery, among others.

"We don't have enough refineries," he warned. Nor did African countries have anywhere near enough storage capacity. Few had as much as 20 days storage.

Addressing the need required much more than just constructing refineries. There was also the need to build the necessary support and downstream infrastructure -- terminals and depots, pipelines, road tanker fleets, service station networks, and gas bottling plants and distribution centres, all the way down to efficient cooking technologies.

"On top of that, we need to look at petrochemicals, at value addition," he stressed. He cited the Indorama Eleme petrochemical plant as a major Nigerian success story.

"Economic development is more important right now for us than the energy transition," averred Kragha. Nevertheless, he also stressed that the transition to green energies presented real opportunities for ARDA's members, that should be seized.

"Are we looking at [sustainable aviation fuel -- SAF] opportunities?" he queried. Were African refiners looking to modify their plants to produce SAF? Further, the shipping sector was now also looking for alternative, low-carbon, fuels to power their vessels, again offering great opportunities for the African sector.

"Energy security is critical to Africa's industrialisation ambitions," he asserted.

The African Petroleum Producers Organisation (APPO) pledged its support for the expansion of African refining capacity. So assured APPO secretary-general Farid Ghezali, addressing the same conference.

He highlighted that currently Africa exported 75% of its petroleum as crude, while importing 70% of its fuel. The effect was to cost the continent $50-billion a year. This meant less development, inadequate industrialisation, fewer jobs, and vulnerability to global political crises.

To be competitive, a refinery needed a minimum capacity of 150 000 bb/d. It had to be integrated with a petrochemicals plant, be ESG- (environmental, social and governance-) certified and be able to meet Euro-6 standards.

Currently, in all of Africa, there were only two global major refinery complexes. These were Nigeria's 650 000 bbl/d Dangote refinery and Algeria's 500 000 bbl/d Sonatrach refinery.

APPO was proposing the development of five major refining hubs across the continent. In addition to Algeria (North Africa) and Nigeria (West Africa), these were Angola (Central Africa), South Africa (Southern Africa) and Tanzania (East Africa). For Angola, APPO was proposing an expansion of refining capacity to 300 000 bbl/d by 2030; for South Africa, the proposal was a capacity of 400 000 bbl/d by 2035, and for Tanzania, 350 000 bbl/d by 2032.

Ghezali suggested that all these refineries be owned 51% by their host States and 49% by the private sector, preferably African investors. They also needed to be integrated into petrochemicals industries, with 30% of their output going to petrochemicals.

By 2035, Africa should be able to refine 3 000 000 bbl/d, in the process creating 500 000 direct and 2 000 000 indirect jobs and retain $100-billion in value in Africa. As for now, Ghezali affirmed ARDA should be able to develop regional roadmaps, start mobilising funding (via the African Energy Bank), and be harmonising standards, by the end of this year.

APPO and ARDA together, he stated, would achieve African industrialisation.

description:
FincoEnergies and Scan Global Logistics (SGL) are expanding their collaboration to roll out a biofuel-based decarbonization solution for road transportation.
The partnership builds on a pilot project launched in 2023, which tested insetting approaches for road transportation.
Martin Andersen, global head of sustainability and ESG at Scan Global Logistics, said, “FincoEnergies is a leading expert in biofuel solutions.
Sophia Carrillo Beeck, senior commercial manager for carbon management at FincoEnergies, said, “Biofuel Swap makes emission reductions tangible and traceable.

text:
FincoEnergies and Scan Global Logistics (SGL) are expanding their collaboration to roll out a biofuel-based decarbonization solution for road transportation.

The initiative, known as Biofuel Swap, enables logistics customers to reduce emissions through the use of certified HVO100 fuel without requiring changes to vehicles, infrastructure or day-to-day operations. The solution is designed to provide verified and scalable CO₂e reductions across global supply chains.

The partnership builds on a pilot project launched in 2023, which tested insetting approaches for road transportation. Following that trial, the companies are moving ahead with broader implementation of the Biofuel Swap model.

Martin Andersen, global head of sustainability and ESG at Scan Global Logistics, said, “FincoEnergies is a leading expert in biofuel solutions. Their expertise and reliable supply enable us to offer a high-quality solution to our customers that can help reduce road transport emissions easily, immediately, and worldwide.”

The Biofuel Swap model is based on a book-and-claim system, in which HVO100 fuel is physically used in trucks operating in the Netherlands, while the associated emissions reductions are allocated to customers elsewhere. This approach is intended to address the limited availability of renewable fuels across transportation networks and the challenges of deploying them directly within all fleets.

According to the companies, the system provides traceable and verified emissions data that can be integrated into customer reporting, including Scope 3 emissions.

Sophia Carrillo Beeck, senior commercial manager for carbon management at FincoEnergies, said, “Biofuel Swap makes emission reductions tangible and traceable. With Scan Global Logistics’ worldwide customer base and global network, the Biofuel Swap solution will have a broad reach.”

The companies said the solution is aimed at closing the gap between decarbonization targets and practical implementation in the road transportation sector, which remains heavily reliant on fossil fuels.

HVO100 used within the program is produced from waste and residue streams and certified under EU-approved schemes such as ISCC, RSB or REDcert. It can deliver up to 90% well-to-wheel CO₂e reductions compared with fossil diesel, according to the companies.

Biofuel Swap will form part of SGL’s broader low-carbon transportation offering, which also includes ocean biofuel, sustainable aviation fuel and electric vehicle solutions.

text:
South Africa’s sugar industry is renewing its push for protection, diversification and long-term sustainability after government and key industry stakeholders signed the second phase of the sector’s masterplan, a move industry leaders say could help stabilize a value chain that supports more than a million livelihoods.

Speaking to CNBC Africa, Andrew Russell, vice chairman of the South African Canegrowers’ Association, said the latest agreement marked an important step forward for an industry that has endured several difficult years marked by economic pressure, import competition and rising input costs.

Russell said the sugar cane value chain had faced “tumultuous times” in recent years, but the signing of the next phase of the masterplan reflects a broad commitment from government, growers, millers and downstream users — including retailers and food and beverage manufacturers — to support the sector’s recovery.

The original masterplan was launched in 2019 after the Department of Trade and Industry and the Department of Agriculture recognized the strategic importance of the sugar industry to rural economies and employment. According to Russell, the second phase builds on that foundation, acknowledging that not all objectives were achieved in the first round and that deeper implementation is now required.

“This second phase recognizes that we didn’t get it all done in the first phase, and there’s still a lot of work to be done,” Russell said. “It’s an extension of that first phase with some renewed commitments and some renewed vigor.”

At the center of the updated framework is a stronger focus on diversification beyond traditional sugar and molasses production. Russell said research undertaken during the first phase explored ways to extract greater value from the entire sugar cane plant, especially through the development of biofuels, sustainable aviation fuel and bioplastics.

That shift is increasingly relevant as global energy prices remain elevated and South African producers grapple with sharply higher diesel costs. Diesel is a critical input for cane farming, affecting both large-scale and small-scale growers, and Russell warned that surging fuel prices are adding to already severe margin pressure across the industry.

He argued that one of the most immediate policy interventions needed is an update to South Africa’s sugar tariff system. The current tariff, which is dollar-based, has not been revised since 2018, according to Russell, and no longer offers sufficient protection against heavily subsidized imports.

The industry’s position is that sugar-producing countries around the world routinely support their domestic sectors through subsidies and special interventions, allowing excess sugar to be sold on the world market at prices South African producers cannot match. As a result, imported sugar enters the domestic market at lower prices, while local producers are pushed into exporting sugar at a loss.

Russell identified Brazil as the main source of imported sugar entering South Africa, with additional shipments coming from parts of the Far East. He said the volume of subsidized imports has become a serious threat to the viability of local production.

“The time is right now for that tariff to be revised and reviewed because it’s not providing the protection that is needed,” Russell said.

According to Russell, the industry submitted an application for a tariff review roughly two years ago. Government has acknowledged the request and is conducting an independent review. The sector is now hoping for an outcome by the end of May.

Alongside tariff reform, the second phase of the masterplan also reinforces commitments around responsible local pricing and encourages domestic users to prioritize South African sugar over imported alternatives. That buy-local commitment is viewed as a key pillar of the social compact underpinning the plan.

For the industry, however, the broader opportunity lies in using current pressures to accelerate structural change. Russell said the fuel crisis could become a turning point if policymakers act quickly to unlock sugar cane’s potential as an energy feedstock.

He argued that ethanol produced from sugar cane could be used in motor vehicles, while more advanced refining could support sustainable aviation fuel production. At current oil prices, he said, such bio-based fuels are becoming increasingly competitive and could help South Africa build a more secure and locally sourced energy supply.

That argument appears to be gaining traction within government. Russell said the industry has received a “sympathetic ear” from officials, noting that Deputy Minister for Trade and Industry Fikile Majola recently visited several sugar mills in KwaZulu-Natal and Mpumalanga to assess the sector’s challenges and opportunities firsthand. Russell said the visit reflected government interest in the strategic role of sugar cane in regional economies and its potential contribution to industrial development.

The biofuels discussion also fits into a broader global trend toward diversification in response to energy market volatility. As economies seek alternatives to crude oil and work to improve energy security, industries such as sugar may find themselves at the center of new investment and policy attention.

Still, the success of South Africa’s sugar masterplan will likely depend on execution. The renewed commitments by industry and government may provide a roadmap, but growers remain under pressure from import competition, outdated tariff protections and rising operating costs.

For now, the signing of the second phase offers the sector a measure of optimism. If tariff relief is granted, local procurement commitments are honored and diversification projects move from research into implementation, South Africa’s sugar industry could shift from survival mode toward a more resilient future.

For a sector that remains deeply tied to rural jobs, agricultural output and industrial activity, the stakes are high. And with fuel prices exposing the vulnerabilities of import dependence, the industry is making the case that sugar cane should no longer be viewed only as a food commodity, but as a strategic economic asset.

Abstract

The development of bioenergy crops on saline–alkaline land has been recognized as a potential pathway for both land restoration and combating global warming. However, the role of soil organic carbon (SOC) dynamics under such conditions remains insufficiently quantified in long-term assessments. In this study, an exploratory assessment was conducted to evaluate the long-term soil carbon sequestration (SCS) potential and life-cycle greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) produced from Arundo donax in the Bohai Rim region of China. The CENTURY model was integrated with Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) time series forecasting to simulate SOC dynamics under future climate scenarios (2024–2035). Compared with the original CENTURY simulation, the LSTM model yielded a substantially more conservative estimate of SOC accumulation, with an Ensemble Mean SCS rate of 0.032 t C/ha/a and a 95% confidence interval ranging from −0.079 to 0.143 t C/ha/a. This result indicates a positive regional average tendency toward soil carbon sequestration, while also suggesting that some locations may behave as carbon sources under less favorable climatic conditions. The total SCS potential across the study area was estimated at 0.615 Tg C. When these soil carbon benefits were incorporated into the life-cycle assessment of Fischer–Tropsch (F-T) SAF, the pathway could become potentially net-negative under the adopted assumptions, reaching −32.1 g CO2e/MJ, which corresponds to a potential reduction of 136.1% relative to fossil aviation fuel. These results should be interpreted as exploratory and scenario-based, given that large-scale cultivation of Arundo donax has not yet been established in the Bohai Rim region and the assessment therefore relies on assumptions. Beyond GHG mitigation, the cultivation of Arundo donax on degraded saline–alkaline soils may also have potential relevance to broader sustainability objectives, including SDG 13 (Climate Action) and SDG 15 (Life on Land). These findings highlight the possible synergies among energy crop cultivation, soil restoration, and climate neutrality goals, and provide preliminary insights for integrating marginal land utilization into sustainable land management and low-carbon aviation strategies.

Growing e-commerce demand and fragmented passenger markets are driving the need for smaller, “right-sized” aircraft to serve low-density and remote regions efficiently.

Compatibility with Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) and fuel-efficient design support lower emissions, allowing airlines to balance sustainability with profitability on thin regional routes.

As global e-commerce expands and regional connectivity becomes more critical, airlines face an evolving challenge: serving thinly populated and infrastructure-constrained regions efficiently, sustainably, and reliably. Traditional large regional jets or turboprops often prove uneconomical on these routes, leaving operators to balance cost, performance, and community service. The D328eco® turboprop from Deutsche Aircraft reflects a new generation of “right-sized” aircraft designed for these conditions.

Driving change

Regional aviation is experiencing a dual shift. On the cargo side, e-commerce growth is creating demand in locations where road or rail logistics cannot meet the speed or frequency required. “Remote communities increasingly rely on air cargo as their lifeline for essential goods and medical supplies,” said Nils Heuer, Director of Global Sales at Deutsche Aircraft. “Operators need aircraft that can serve small parcels and time-sensitive freight efficiently. Large aircraft cannot economically meet these needs.”

Passenger demand is following a similar pattern of fragmentation. Many routes cannot justify large aircraft, yet communities still require dependable access to regional hubs. “Thin passenger routes require high-frequency services with aircraft that are flexible and efficient,” Heuer explained. “This is especially true for areas with dispersed populations. The D328eco’s 40-seat design aligns perfectly with these evolving demands.”

Remote and constrained airports

Regions such as northern Canada and rural Australia face infrastructure limitations and challenging geography. Short takeoff and landing (STOL) performance allows the D328eco to operate from airfields inaccessible to many other turboprops or regional jets. “Takeoff distances around 1,028 m and landing distances near 965 m open up destinations that were previously unreachable,” Heuer noted. “Gravel runway capability further extends access. Communities benefit from reliable air connectivity even in harsh conditions.”

Similar requirements exist in mountainous northern India and small island airports across Southeast Asia. Limited runway length, low population density, and thin demand make flexible aircraft essential. “Operators need aircraft that can perform reliably on constrained strips,” Heuer added. “STOL capability, combined with efficient turnaround, makes multiple daily rotations feasible. This ensures continuous access for both passengers and cargo.”

Right-sized economics

Low-density cargo operations demand capacity that matches actual freight volumes. Oversized aircraft create unnecessary trip costs, while undersized planes limit commercial viability. “Right-sized payload is key for sustainability,” Heuer stated. “The D328eco carries exactly what is needed for high-density parcels, medical supplies, and mid-volume freight. This avoids wasted capacity and reduces operational risk.”

The modular cabin enables rapid reconfiguration for cargo-only, combi, or passenger-plus-cargo layouts, enhancing flexibility. Efficient ground handling and fast turnarounds support multiple daily rotations on short regional sectors. “Operators can adapt quickly to fluctuating demand,” Heuer said. “This adaptability is critical in remote markets. The aircraft balances payload, economics, and operational reliability seamlessly.”

Enhancing connectivity

Passenger travel in remote locations is often essential for medical, business, educational, and personal needs. Traditional 70-seat turboprops or regional jets are usually too large to operate profitably. “Smaller, high-performance aircraft allow routes that larger platforms cannot economically support,” Heuer explained. “Communities gain reliable scheduled services. Airlines can maintain frequent, low-risk flights on thin routes.”

The D328eco’s 40-seat configuration, STOL performance, and fuel-efficient engines reduce operating costs while expanding connectivity. “High frequency and low trip costs are critical to remote passengers,” Heuer added. “Thin markets benefit when aircraft are optimised for both economics and accessibility. Efficient, right-sized operations become viable where larger aircraft fail.”

Sustainability meets viability

Environmental sustainability is increasingly critical for regional operators. Turboprop engines reduce fuel burn and CO₂ emissions, while full compatibility with 100 percent Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF), including Power-to-Liquid SAF, provides further ecological benefit. “Economic and environmental sustainability must go hand in hand,” Heuer said. “The D328eco supports both. Airlines can reduce emissions without compromising profitability.”

Fuel-efficient engines and modern avionics enable reliable operations even on thin regional routes. “Operators no longer have to choose between green initiatives and financial viability,” Heuer continued. “Sustainable operations are achievable on every route. Communities gain consistent service with minimal environmental impact.”

Approximately 100,000 litres of used cooking oil annually is transformed into sustainable aviation fuel and renewable diesel

Pursuing luxury with purpose, Marina Bay Sands has advanced its environmental commitment as the first Asian hospitality organisation to establish a closed loop in renewable fuel, reimagining everyday waste as a powerful source of low-carbon energy.

Approximately 100,000 litres of used cooking oil from Marina Bay Sands’ kitchens are diverted annually, transformed into sustainable aviation fuel and renewable diesel in partnership with Neste, one of the world’s largest refineries for sustainable aviation fuel and renewable diesel production.

How this works

Twice a week, used cooking oil from Marina Bay Sands’ kitchens is collected and stored in dedicated containers before being transported to Neste’s refinery in Singapore. It is then processed alongside other waste streams and residues, processed into high-quality fuel, free from sulphur, oxygen and aromatic compounds. Once refined, the diesel is procured back for operational use to power the property's back-up generators, lowering carbon emissions from this fuel type by 11 per cent.

This initiative is one of the many ways Marina Bay Sands breathes new life into waste, reinforcing its dedication in minimising environmental impact while operating at world-class standards. The transformation of used cooking oil into renewable fuel goes beyond an operational milestone – it sets a new benchmark for responsible luxury and world-class hospitality.

Closing the need-solution gap in road transport decarbonisation

The road transport sector remains heavily reliant on fossil fuels, while continuing to struggle with the limited availability of sustainable fuels, such as HVO, along key routes. text:
Cruise lines are altering Alaska itineraries weeks before the region's cruise season begins, swapping out visits to Tracy Arm Fjord for nearby Endicott Arm Fjord.

A landslide above the toe of the South Sawyer Glacier in the Tracy Arm Fjord caused a tsunami last Aug. 10, and the U.S. Geological Survey warns it is still a hazardous area.

"Steep, mountainous landslide areas are inherently unstable and will continue to change for years following an initial landslide," the Geological Survey said on its website. "Continued rockfall and smaller-scale landslide events from the exposed landslide scar are expected and could impact the water, potentially causing future local tsunamis. As such, this area remains hazardous."

At least seven cruise lines have said they will not sail in Tracy Arm this year: Carnival, Royal Caribbean, Virgin Voyages, MSC, Oceania, Holland America Line and Windstar. Tracy Arm is a popular area for scenic cruising and glacier viewing.

All seven cruise lines will instead visit Endicott Arm Fjord, which features Dawes Glacier. The two neighboring fjords are about 50 miles south of Juneau.

Endicott Arm is a wider waterway, and Dawes Glacier sits at the end of it. Tracy Arm is narrower and features the North and South Sawyer Glaciers.

The Southeast Alaska Pilots' Association, which helps cruise ships navigate the region, did not respond to a request for comment, but a spokesperson for Oceania Cruises said the association feels "that it's not safe to transit Tracy Arm."

Several cruise lines, including National Geographic-Lindblad Expeditions, have not made itinerary adjustments.

A spokesperson for National Geographic-Lindblad said, "We are currently monitoring conditions but have no plans to deviate from current calls at this time."

If clients ask about the itinerary change, advisors can point to the Geological Survey's recommendation and that the cruise lines are "putting the passengers and their safety first," said Allison Roth, a travel consultant with Brentwood Travel in St. Louis.

Many first-time cruisers to Alaska don't know how the Tracy Arm and Endicott Arm glacier-viewing experiences compare, said Nancy Winter, a Maple Grove, Minn.-based advisor with Travel Leaders Market Square. That may mean that when itinerary swaps happen, "they don't really know they're having a different experience" than what they originally booked, she said.

Advisors can communicate the Endicott switch as an opportunity to see a different Alaskan landscape, she suggested.

Winter recalled sailing Endicott Arm last year with Celebrity Cruises and said her fjord visit was about four and a half hours. The scenery included waterfalls cascading down the cliffs.

"It's pretty, and then you get to the end, where the glacier is," she said. "It's kind of like a hallway that you're cruising down."

Though Endicott Arm is now serving as an alternative for Tracy Arm, the latter was already an alternative for Glacier Bay National Park.

The park features multiple glacier viewings and a wider waterway than the fjords. But the National Park Service limits how many cruise lines can visit seasonally and how many cruise ships can enter daily.

As more cruise lines sail Alaska, more cruise guests are naturally being funneled to alternative scenic-cruising destinations.

MSC Cruises and Virgin Voyages, for example, are sailing Alaska for the first time this year and both had planned to sail Tracy Arm Fjord but are now headed to Endicott.

According to CLIA, there will be six more ships in Alaska this year compared to last year.

Vertical Aerospace stock represents one of the most watched opportunities in the burgeoning Advanced Air Mobility (AAM) sector. Company Background and Public Listing

Founding and Mission

Founded in 2016 by Stephen Fitzpatrick, Vertical Aerospace was established with the mission to make air travel personal, on-demand, and carbon-free. Business Operations and Growth Drivers

Flagship Aircraft: The VX4

The primary driver of Vertical Aerospace stock value is the VX4. This eVTOL aircraft is designed to carry a pilot and four passengers over ranges of up to 100 miles at speeds exceeding 150 mph. One of the company's most significant assets is its commercial momentum. As of recent filings, Vertical Aerospace boasts a conditional pre-order book of over 1,500 aircraft, valued at approximately $6 billion. This pipeline provides a roadmap for future revenue once certification is achieved.

Flight Testing Program

Vertical Aerospace continues to hit technical milestones. In 2024, the company successfully conducted piloted transition flights, a critical step where the aircraft moves from vertical lift to forward wing-borne flight. The timeline for commercialization depends on Type Certification from the CAA and EASA (European Union Aviation Safety Agency). Currently, Vertical Aerospace aims for certification by 2027-2028. For investors, each successful regulatory audit serves as a potential catalyst for the stock price.
